Description
PhD Student – Mammal Community Ecology
The Shared Planet Group led by Dr. Alex Jensen and based at Texas State University is recruiting a PhD student to start August 2027. This PhD student’s research will focus on mammal responses to resource pulses, with field work likely primarily occurring somewhat locally. There is funding available for 4.5 years.

The core of this PhD project will consist of collecting observational and experimental data on mammal responses to resource pulses in the field. Examples of locally important resource pulses include persimmons, prickly pear, and acorns. Several approaches will likely be used to study these interactions, including camera traps, selective exclusion, and scat surveys. The PhD student will also be expected to lead a paper (one of their chapters) that complements their field project but utilizes existing large-scale data or synthesizes existing research.

The PhD student will be expected to mentor undergraduate students, be a collaborative member of our research group, and participate in Biology Department activities. There are funds to attend one national conference and one regional conference per year. Alex encourages people from a wide range of backgrounds and experiences to apply but can only consider international applicants that are already living in the US. The PhD student will not have to pay tuition but will be expected to teach (TA) during 4 semesters.

Logistics
To apply: Fill out this Google form by September 30

Description
Description: I am recruiting one MS student to participate in an ongoing multi-year (2027-2029) project to assess population sizes, demographics, reproductive rates, growth rates, and survivorship of freshwater turtle populations in Mississippi. This will entail extensive trapping surveys, including mark-recapture, to capture, mark, and measure freshwater turtles, including at-risk and federally listed species. Together with an established doctoral student, the successful applicant will conduct repeated trapping and snorkel surveys at up to 12 established long-term monitoring sites in Mississippi for the alligator snapping turtle, Pascagoula map turtle, Pearl River map turtle, and other freshwater turtle species. We will also gather demographic information, including but not limited to survival and growth rates across size and sex classes, sex ratios, and clutch sizes. Data from these surveys will be used to estimate population density and assess population trends and extinction risk under different scenarios, using population viability analyses. Captured turtles will also be scanned for the presence of ingested fishhooks, so we can monitor the effects of these on individual health and survivorship. Mississippi boasts a high biodiversity of chelonians, including multiple species that are federally and state listed, or of conservation concern, and multiple single river endemic species. The information gained from this study will inform population viability analyses and other assessments for these freshwater turtle species, especially those of conservation concern. 
 Qualifications: Applicants must have a BS in ecology/environmental biology, zoology, wildlife biology, or other relevant areas. Academic record(s) must be competitive for admission to the University of Southern Mississippi graduate program in Biology. Prior experience with the safe operation of small motorboats and with trapping/handling of aquatic turtles is preferred but not required. Willingness and ability to work with a partner (for safety) is a must, as is the ability to conduct field work under potentially challenging field conditions, including high heat and humidity. 
 Application: To apply, please send the following: cover letter, resume or CV, unofficial transcripts, and contact information for three references to Professor Carl Qualls, Carl.Qualls@usm.edu.  Also address any inquiries about the position to the same address. GRE scores are not required, but if already taken, applicants may also send an unofficial copy of GRE scores. A start date of January 2027 and enrollment for the Spring 2027 semester is anticipated. Review of applications will begin immediately and will continue until the position is filled.
  Contact
Carl Qualls

Carl.Qualls@usm.edu (preferred contact method)

Description
The Lowman Lab in the School of Aquatic and Fishery Sciences (SAFS) at the University of Washington (UW) is recruiting a PhD student in watershed ecology and biogeochemistry to start in fall 2027. Applicants should be interested in conducting research on topics including, but not limited to, quantifying recovery and resilience of streams and rivers following large floods or other disturbances, the effects of wildfire on stream biogeochemistry, how compounding climate events impact aquatic primary productivity and nutrient cycling, how changing winter hydrology and precipitation shapes stream productivity (both primary and secondary), and how human modification of the landscape or flow regime alters stream ecosystem function and biodiversity.
 Graduate students in the Lowman Lab will be trained in foundational stream ecology methods and approaches, field ecology techniques, analytical chemistry protocols, data science and programming for ecological modeling, manuscript preparation, grant writing, and science communication. Students will also be encouraged to attend national and international conferences and workshops to present their findings, build their networks, and identify new career opportunities. At SAFS, the graduate student will join a dynamic and highly collaborative community of aquatic scientists and will have opportunities to join associated programs, such as the Quantitative Ecology and Resource Management Program. 
 Successful candidates will be: enthusiastic about watershed ecology and biogeochemistry; organized and detail-oriented with demonstrated experience managing research projects; and collegial and excited to collaborate as part of larger, multi-disciplinary research groups. Applicants must possess a bachelor’s degree in a relevant field (biology, chemistry, earth/environmental science, etc.) by spring 2027 and a minimum of one year of prior research experience (either in academic or professional settings). The position is funded through a combination of SAFS teaching/research assistantships, including a paid stipend, tuition waiver, and health insurance. There is also a possibility for the student to begin developing project ideas and gain experience as a field research technician in summer 2027.
 Interested applicants should submit a one-page cover letter (describing past experience, motivation to pursue a graduate degree, and reasons for applying to this position), a CV or resume, an unofficial transcript, and contact information for three professional references via e-mail to Dr. Heili Lowman (hlowman@uw.edu) by October 9. Dr. Lowman is committed to building equitable, supportive research communities and strongly encourages applications from candidates with a diversity of experiences, interests, and identities. Applicants whose skills and interests best align with the research team will be invited to conduct video interviews with Dr. Lowman in mid-October, and competitive applicants will be invited to submit their applications to the UW SAFS program (due November 15). Note, SAFS does not require applicants to have taken the GRE. Please reach out to Dr. Lowman with any questions regarding the application, graduate programs, the lab group, or research projects.
Contact
Heili Lowman
hlowman@uw.edu (preferred contact method)

Description
The Wilson lab in the Department of Entomology at the University of Kentucky is recruiting a PhD or MS student in Entomology to start in Spring 2027. This position will be located in Lexington, Kentucky on the main campus of the University of Kentucky. We study sustainable insect pest management and natural enemy conservation in urban trees, shrubs, and turfgrass. The selected student would be expected to study 1) how flowering lawn weeds influence biological control of scale insects in urban trees, and 2) the degree to which lawn-applied insecticides translocate into scale honeydew in nearby trees and resultant effects on natural enemy communities. The selected student will be encouraged to develop their own research projects under the general themes of the lab.
  Ideal applicants will possess an MS degree if applying to be a PhD student and a BS degree if applying to be an MS student. Candidates should have a background in entomology, ecology, environmental sciences, biology, or a related field. Prior experience with field-based data collection, scientific writing, and statistical analysis are preferred. Successful applicants will start in January 2027. Students will receive an assistantship which fully covers tuition and provides a competitive stipend and health insurance. Prospective applicants are encouraged to contact Dr. Caleb Wilson with questions: c.wilson@uky.edu
 The University of Kentucky is located in Lexington, Kentucky which contains a vibrant downtown along with many excellent options for dining, shopping, and outdoor recreation. The department of entomology is composed of 20 faculty with expertise in a wide array of disciplines. The department is consistently ranked as one of the most productive in the country and our students have moved on to successful careers in academia, industry, and government. Starting in December 2026, the department will be based in the newly constructed Agricultural Research Building which will contain state-of-the-art lab equipment for conducting research.
 Additional information can be found at the Wilson lab website: https://caleb-j-wilson.com/, and the University of Kentucky Department of Entomology graduate program: https://entomology.ca.uky.edu/academics/graduate. 
 Prospective students should email application materials to Dr. Caleb Wilson at c.wilson@uky.edu by September 18th, 2026. Interviews will be conducted as applications are received. Lab: The Nancy Fair Link Laminitis Research Center at the Mississippi State University College of Veterinary Medicine is dedicated to improving the prevention, diagnosis and management of equine laminitis. The Center benefits from a collaborative environment that bridges fundamental research and clinical application. It is equipped with state-of-the-art facilities to support research across the full spectrum of laminitis: from the molecular mechanisms to the development of new diagnostic tools and management strategies.

Project: Insulin dysregulation is an endocrine disease resulting in hyperinsulinemia and a major risk factor for endocrinopathic laminitis. Description
M.S. or Ph.D. Assistantship at U of Wyoming studying the importance of mesic habitats for ungulate conservation  
The Merkle Research Group is looking for a highly motivated, creative, and quantitative M.S. or Ph.D. student to lead a project studying how ungulates use and rely on mesic habitats, as well as studying how to prioritize mesic habitat restoration to benefit ungulate populations. 

The project is a collaboration between Working Lands for Wildlife, Wyoming Cooperative Fish and Wildlife Research Unit, and University of Wyoming. The primary goal of the project is purposefully broad, and the student will have the opportunity to shape their specific research questions accordingly. The research will primarily rely on previously collected GPS collar and remote sensing data related to mesic areas (see https://www.mesic.app/), and the position will have a heavy emphasis on data analytics over field work.

Candidates must have a B.S. and preferably a M.S. degree (for starting as a Ph.D. student) in Ecology, Wildlife, Computing, or related field. Applicants with experience managing and analyzing large spatial datasets (including remote sensing and animal movement data) in program R, working independently and with a team on research projects, and publishing peer-reviewed research will be favored. Successful applicants will be expected to participate in a collaborative team environment, co-produce high-quality research, present their work at professional conferences, and publish results in a timely manner in peer-reviewed journals. 

The successful applicant will be admitted through the Program in Ecology and Evolution at University of Wyoming and be based in Laramie (USA). A graduate assistantship will be provided, which includes tuition and benefits, and a monthly stipend of $2,000/month (M.S.) or $2,418/month (Ph.D.). To apply, please email a SINGLE PDF file that includes 1) a detailed cover letter outlining, at a minimum, experience and interest in studying habitat conservation as it relates to ungulates and analyzing animal movement data, 2) a CV, 3) contact information for three references, and 4) unofficial transcripts to Dr. Jerod Merkle (jmerkle@uwyo.edu) and Dr. Julie Brockman (jbrockm1@uwyo.edu). Review of applicants will begin October 5. Start date is negotiable but January 2027 is preferred. 

Contact
Julia Brockman
jbrockm1@uwyo.edu (preferred contact method)

Description
A Master of Science (M.S.) position is available at Auburn University. The incoming student will be a Graduate Research Assistant in Dr. Tim Bruce’s Fish Health Lab within the School of Fisheries, Aquaculture and Aquatic Sciences (SFAAS). Research in the Bruce lab focuses on host-pathogen interactions in cultured fish species, nutritional aspects of fish health, and fish vaccines/therapeutants.
 Responsibilities and tasks 
This M.S. project will involve experimental laboratory studies (~80%) and in vivo trial work with warmwater fish species (~20%). Specifically, this M.S. thesis research will examine microbial interactions using molecular techniques. The bacterial species involved in this project are relevant to U.S. aquaculture (catfish, largemouth bass, and tilapia), and the project will involve genomic and proteomic analyses. Overall, the student will be expected to conduct an independent research project, followed by the writing and defense of a detailed thesis.  

Qualifications 
The Bruce Fish Health Lab team is looking for a motivated candidate who has:

•   Bachelor’s degree in Microbiology/Biological Sciences 
•   Detailed knowledge of microbiology and/or fish health/immunology 
•   Proven ability to carry out goal-oriented work and fluent with data management systems and programming software 
•   Lab competencies in microbiology (e.g., culture, identification, sequencing, microbial-based assays)  
•   Molecular biology skills (e.g., SDS-PAGE/Western blot, gene expression [qPCR], proteomics) are also required. 
•   Assistance with fish husbandry and conducting aquaculture trials is also required 
•   Ability to work independently and in a team laboratory setting

The College of Southern Nevada (CSN) is seeking a full-time, tenure-track Instructor in Organismal Biology to provide instruction in biology and organismal biology-related coursework and support student achievement and success while contributing to the College’s commitment to excellence in teaching and learning. 

The Department of Biological Sciences provides quality instruction for courses required by limited-entry programs in Health Sciences, the Associate of Science Degree in Biology, and the Bachelor of Applied Science (BAS) in Environmental Conservation. The Department currently has a strong focus on increasing student throughput into limited-entry Health Sciences programs and supporting the growth of the BAS in Environmental Conservation.

·        Participating in discipline, department, and school meetings and activities

·        Serving on department, school, and college-wide committees that focus on unit planning and institutional decision-making.

·        Establishing and maintaining positive working relationships with students, faculty, and staff of diverse ethnic, cultural, and socioeconomic backgrounds.

Description
 The Wildlife Ecology Laboratory (WEL) at Tennessee State University (TSU) is seeking a post-doctoral research associate to utilize environmental DNA as an early screening tool for aquatic invasive species in National Forests throughout the southeast United States. In addition to refining molecular approaches to screen for aquatic invasive species, the project will aim to compare eDNA screening approaches to traditional aquatic survey methods. The postdoc will work collaboratively with researchers from the USDA Forest Service Southern Research Station and Clemson University and will be expected to lead research efforts related to sample processing and post-processing of genome-scale bioinformatics data. The successful candidate will be expected to assist with mentoring graduate and undergraduate students in the WEL. In addition to the primary project responsibilities, there will be opportunities to assist with other ongoing wildlife research projects. 

Applicants must hold a PhD in a relevant field and have a demonstrated record of peer-reviewed publications, including at least one first author publication. Required skillsets include strong writing and quantitative skills, and prior experience with molecular approaches, including quantitative PCR, metabarcoding, and post-processing of genome-scale bioinformatics data. Other preferred skillsets include proficiency with the R statistical analysis platform and prior experience with occupancy and species distribution models. 
 Employment is contingent upon successfully completing a criminal background check as mandated by Tennessee State University.
Official transcripts for positions which require a post-secondary undergraduate degree, advanced degree and/or certification must be presented upon hire.

An unofficial transcript may be attached in the “Transcript” section.
You will be required to provide names and contact information for three references during your application to the posting. If you are the recommended candidate for the position, our online hiring system will automatically generate solicitation for these letters using contact information you provided.

Description
 *Applications are reviewed on a rolling-basis.

ARS Office/Lab and Location: A research opportunity is currently available with the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA), Agricultural Research Service (ARS), San Joaquin Valley Agricultural Sciences Center, in Parlier, California.

The Agricultural Research Service (ARS) is the U.S. Department of Agriculture's chief scientific in-house research agency with a mission to find solutions to agricultural problems that affect Americans every day from field to table. ARS will deliver cutting-edge, scientific tools and innovative solutions for American farmers, producers, industry, and communities to support the nourishment and well-being of all people; sustain our nation’s agroecosystems and natural resources; and ensure the economic competitiveness and excellence of our agriculture. The vision of the agency is to provide global leadership in agricultural discoveries through scientific excellence.

The San Joaquin Valley Agricultural Sciences Center conducts research to support the sustainability, quality, and productivity of specialty crops industries across California’s Central Valley. The Commodity Protection and Quality Research Unit focuses on improving postharvest quality and reducing losses of horticultural specialty crops caused by fungal pathogens, physiological disorders, and the control of quarantine insect pests that threaten market access and export opportunities.

Research Project: We are seeking a highly motivated postdoctoral fellow to be a part of research focused on postharvest disease management and quality of fresh fruits. The fellowship has two primary learning experiences. You will examine the susceptibility of table grape breeding lines to gray mold caused by Botrytis cinerea, including developing and conducting scalable, high-throughput phenotyping methods to assess susceptibility and evaluate established or newly developed screening approaches. This also includes developing and evaluating preharvest and postharvest treatments aimed at controlling postharvest diseases of fresh fruits. This offers opportunities to contribute to high-value research that directly supports industry resilience and helps strengthen postharvest disease control.

Learning Objectives: Under the guidance of the mentor, you will:

Learn to conduct research focused on postharvest disease management and quality in fresh fruits.
Gain experience evaluating the susceptibility of table grape breeding lines to gray mold caused by Botrytis cinerea.
Develop skills in designing and implementing scalable, high-throughput phenotyping methods to assess disease susceptibility.
Learn to evaluate and refine established and newly developed screening approaches for postharvest disease resistance.
Build experience in developing and assessing preharvest and postharvest treatments to control postharvest diseases in fresh fruit.
Mentor(s): The mentor for this opportunity is Seiya Saito (seiya.saito@usda.gov). If you have questions about the nature of the research, please contact the mentor(s).

Anticipated Appointment Start Date: Fall 2026. Start date is flexible and will depend on a variety of factors.

Appointment Length: The appointment will initially be for one year, but may be renewed upon recommendation of ARS and is contingent on the availability of funds.

Level of Participation: The appointment is full time.

Participant Stipend: The participant will receive a monthly stipend commensurate with educational level and experience. The anticipated stipend is $75,000 annually.

Citizenship Requirements: This opportunity is available to U.S. citizens only.

ORISE Information: This program, administered by ORAU through its contract with the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) to manage the Oak Ridge Institute for Science and Education (ORISE), was established through an interagency agreement between DOE and ARS. Participants do not become employees of USDA, ARS, DOE or the program administrator, and there are no employment-related benefits. Proof of health insurance is required for participation in this program. Health insurance can be obtained through ORISE.

Questions: Please visit our Program Website. After reading, if you have additional questions about the application process, please email ORISE.ARS.PacificWest@orau.org and include the reference code for this opportunity.

Qualifications
The qualified candidate should have received or be currently pursuing a doctoral degree in one of the relevant fields. Degree must have been received within the past five years, or be currently pursuing.

Please select "Plant Science" as your discipline if your degree is Plant Pathology; Plant Science encompasses Plant Pathology.

Preferred skills:

Experience in plant pathology — Demonstrated hands-on experience in research on fungal diseases, or a closely related field.
Experience with Botrytis species or other fungal pathogens such as Alternaria, Cladosporium, Mucor, or Penicillium is a plus.
Applied research skills — Strong understanding of applied research, including experimental design, data collection, data analysis, and interpretation of results.
Sample management — Experience managing, organizing, and archiving biological samples.
Independent and collaborative research — Ability to conduct research independently and act effectively as part of a diverse research team.

Description
Student Services Contractor: Fish Biologist (Acoustic Telemetry Research)

Fish Telemetry Research | Pacific Northwest

We are seeking a current student or recent graduate (within one year of graduation) to join our team as a service contractor supporting several fish telemetry research projects. This is a unique opportunity to combine hands-on fieldwork with rigorous quantitative research on high-profile fisheries and water management issues.

About the Role

You will conduct field research on juvenile salmon and endangered sucker species in large lakes, reservoirs, and estuaries in the Pacific Northwest. Your work will directly contribute to our understanding of fish habitat use, movement, spatial distribution, and survival of these species. 

This position offers a dynamic, seasonal balance:

Less than half the year: Take a lead role in demanding field operations, deploying and retrieving telemetry equipment and collecting data from boats in dynamic aquatic environments.  Field work requires travel for up to 100 days a year. 
Remainder of the year: Conduct advanced data analysis to interpret spatial distribution and movement patterns of aquatic animals, and contribute to scientific writing.
You will be expected to complete analyses and author or co-author peer-reviewed reports and manuscripts for publication in scientific journals — an excellent opportunity to build your publication record.

Desired Qualifications

Required:

Master's or Ph.D. in Aquatic Ecology, Animal Movement Ecology, Fishery Biology, Aquatic Biology, Biostatistics, or a closely related field
Experience with hazardous outdoor fieldwork conducted from a boat
Extensive experience navigating boats (up to 20 ft) in large water bodies with challenging conditions — current, wind, and tidal dynamics
Formal education/training in statistical methods used to describe animal spatial distribution, movement, and behavior
Expertise in fish telemetry technologies such as Innovasea and JSATS systems
Preferred:

Comfort operating fishing nets and working outdoors in all weather conditions, including hot, cold, wet, dry, windy, and icy environments
Experience as a lead author of scientific publications in peer reviewed journals. 
Location

This is a home-based position, but fieldwork will be conducted out of the Columbia River Research Station in Cook, WA. Applicants must live within approximately a 90-minute drive of this location and should expect to report to the Cook, WA lab throughout the 4–6 month field season.

Timing

Start date: No later than January 4, 2027

Appointment length: One to two years, depending on level of entry

Schedule: 40 hours per week, up to 1,928 hours per year

Salary and Benefits

Pay rate: $41.51–$49.74 per hour

Travel expenses will be paid by USGS

Please note that this is a Student Services Contractor (SSC) position, which differs from a standard employee appointment in the following ways:

SSCs are not eligible to participate in employee medical insurance or retirement plans

SSCs do not receive premium (overtime) pay for work beyond eight hours/day or 40 hours/week

SSCs are paid only for hours actually worked, with no holiday or annual leave benefits

 

Who Should Apply

This position is ideal for a motivated early-career scientist who is comfortable working independently in physically demanding field conditions and who also enjoys the analytical and writing side of research. If you're looking to build real-world experience in fish telemetry, spatial ecology, and scientific publishing, we encourage you to apply.

How to Apply

To apply send resume listing experience, education, publications, and graduation or expected graduation dates to Summer Burdick sburdick@usgs.gov. Applications will be accepted until September 25, 2026.

Contact
Summer Burdick
sburdick@usgs.gov (preferred contact method)
